utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tanaskovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vojinovic.

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shall we start off from where we were yesterday when you said you had weapons and that you used to go home. My question was: Did Mitar Vasiljevic have weapons and if you can remember, what kind of weapon did he have?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mitar had a weapon or not. In the kitchen where I was and while he was with me, I didn't see it because nobody brought weapons into the kitchen. I didn't bring my weapons into the kitchen. There was a sort of storage room. I would leave my automatic rifle there, then I would go into the kitchen and then when I needed it, when I went home, then I would take it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you received those weapons?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that the others also received these weapons, signed for them, and were issued with such weapons?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I asked because I travel for 7 kilometres, I have to go through a wood late at night, and I leave my house early in the morning. I was afraid. The situation was tense. Luckily nothing ever happened to me, and for a while I did carry it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how you and also how Mitar Vasiljevic, what kind of a uniform you wore and what kind of a uniform did Mitar Vasiljevic have, if you had one?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember because it wasn't really my job to look or to remember. I'm a 65-year-old man so I don't remember what kind of a uniform he wore. I don't remember at all and I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a uniform did you have?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning when we first started work, I had a shirt which I used to work in Belgrade, and I had that at home. It was a secondhand one. And I also wore a suit for a while. After a while, we got those multi-coloured suits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "later we received," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that occasionally you would go home.

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vasiljevic Mitar also do that?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic used to do that while he was working with us. He didn't have any transport but he used to go in the evening, he would just report and say, "I have to go and try to stop a car so that I can go home to my children."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was no organised transport?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember, could you please tell us how long Vasiljevic stayed in Prelovo in that kitchen?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he could have stayed for 15 days at the most while we fixed up the kitchen, brought in the stoves. He was there to organise the purchase or how we obtained the stoves, the cleaning. There was a lot of broken stuff in the halls and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated yesterday that you prepared food for the lines, for the positions?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the positions, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, if you can remember, how you took that food out to the lines; lunch, dinner, so on?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent it in 25 kilo cauldrons that we used for cooking. And in the evening, we would send packed food, tins, pates, butter, and then in the morning, we would send out tea and little things like that so that they could have a bite of something before lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the dry food that you sent, did you also make any kind of prepared, cooked foods for dinner?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody said that they wanted something cooked and something was left over, we would send it to those who asked for it. We would also send food a little further out, because the distances were quite long. There were forests there. So further out we would send preserved meat or milk, things that they could prepare for themselves over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make it a little clearer, was cooked food ever taken out to the lines in the evening?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. Maybe we did take that kind of food there sometimes, but I forget things like that. I'm a 65-year-old person. I forget a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we discussed uniforms a little while ago --

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- did you have any insignia on your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you, Mitar did wear some kind of insignia. I don't know how long or wide it was. The people from TO ordered him to -- the people who wore those red ribbons were the only persons who could go into the kitchen and work. Those people who did not have such a ribbon were not allowed to enter into the kitchen, and I think this was for reasons of hygiene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who wore those, as you call them, rags?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I had one, and also all the others who help. I don't know their names. I don't know the young people, because I spent a lot of time in Belgrade, 24 years. So I know a few of the older residents there, but I don't know the soldiers who used to come round and those who used to help us out in the kitchen. I can't remember. I forget things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what those strips of fabric looked like and where you put them on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given one, and I wore it on my shoulder. It was tied right here. And that's what I did. But those who went out to the line, what can I tell you? One day I could see that they wore green ribbons. The next day they wore red ones. What that was, I never asked. I know that we who we were helping out there, we would wear that when we were helping out in the kitchen. Also, this goes for persons who assisted in the kitchen. And when they no longer worked there, they gave them back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a little while ago that Mr. Vasiljevic had something - I'm not sure exactly how you said it - something wider.

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I remember that he and another person who was in charge of the sanitary inspections, and Mitar too, because he was sent there to help us out and to do certain things. And he did help us a lot. So when we finished all the work in the kitchen, when we set it up and when we started to prepare food, later, Mitar left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, that thing that Mitar had, can you please explain? Was that a piece of fabric? a rag? Was it a ribbon? Was it something else?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was something that was three fingers wide that he wore around his arm, and it was red. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something that comes from your -- what you said yesterday. Could you please tell us the following -- well, you said now "later, Mitar left." Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything. I know about him while we were together at Prelovo. He would come. He wore that ribbon which indicated that he was permitted to enter into the kitchen, as well as the others who wore that. After that -- I don't know anything about Mitar after he left Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about what happened to him later?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps after awhile there were stories circulating around that he had an accident, that he had broken his leg, but I didn't see him when he broke his leg. I didn't go to the town. I was tied to the kitchen. I couldn't go because I was responsible in the kitchen for the food. It couldn't be late. It couldn't be late in arriving out in the field and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that there were two vans there. So I would like to ask you now, at what time do you remember that there were two of these vans? And this relates to Prelovo and Blace.

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mitar left, they gave us a van, a small truck - I can't remember - that we used to transport the food, because these were quite some distances. The van was from the forestry unit. I just said a van. I didn't even look at it really. My assistants would carry the food out and put it inside, and I would stay inside, and I would be preparing the food for people who were around us as well. Once I took the cauldrons out, I can't remember whether it was a van or a little truck. It was a small vehicle that you could put cauldrons in in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, the van that you call a van or a small truck, it came after Mr. Vasiljevic left?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, did you hear or see any army that did not belong to regular army units, something that we call paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I had nothing to do with that. My job was to work in the kitchen, to make sure that everything was on time, because we didn't have electric stoves. We used wood for burning, and it wasn't an organised, proper kitchen. But only because I was an older military chef. I did my best. I had to hurry. I asked for all kinds of wood in order to be able to do what I could do. I never left the kitchen. I don't know who was coming and going, what people were doing, what kind of an army was there, and I really wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard that Mr. Vasiljevic was arrested.

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel about that and how did all these people in your area feel about that?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, we were all surprised and we were all sorry. We were sorry and we were wondering about it and we're still wondering about it today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you wondering about it?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we know Mitar. He would pass by my house to go to school. I know his parents. I never heard anything bad about him, not in his youth or at dances. When I would come home, I never heard that something happened. Everything was quite usual, and I don't really know. I know what I know. There's not much I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you know both Mr. Vasiljevic and his father. You know his village. Could you please tell us your opinion; what kind of a family is this?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar comes from a good family, and his whole village, when I happened to be there, when I come from Belgrade, when they celebrate St. George's day, they were very nice people. We never had any kind of bad relations with them. His father was a good man, a good householder, a good worker. To this very day, he is still running around and working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this news probably surprised you and made you wonder.

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Since we know that Mitar, in his youth, never created any problems in our area, and I can say that. When we heard about it, we were surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, perhaps, just one more question which I failed to do in that context when we were talking about that topic. Yesterday, you mentioned (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This (redacted), did he drive that, as you call it, van or small truck? And did (redacted), was (redacted) with you from the beginning or was it at some other time?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the beginning. He was there later on. After Mitar left, he came to us. Where he went later, I don't know, but I know that when Mitar left, because he helped to run things and he helped us about the goods and the cauldrons and the stoves, and he found a way for us to clean the corridors so that they would be clean and that's why he introduced the insignia so that not everybody could come in. This was strictly forbidden. Once he left, then this (redacted) came, his name is (redacted), and his nickname is (redacted), but I never called him (redacted) I always called him (redacted). I am an older man, but perhaps his colleagues used his nickname (redacted), but I called him (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from before or not?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you briefly tell us what kind of a man is he?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not a bad man. He's an honest man. I don't know in which state he works. He works there today. He would come home. He's a good host. He has a nice home, a wife, children. He's not a very heavy, large man. He is from a poor family, but now he has a home of his own. That's all I know about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your opinion, he's an honest man?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know anything else about him?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vojinovic, my name is Dermot Groome and I'm representing the Prosecutor, and I will ask you a few questions regarding your testimony.

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how long, all together, did you work in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that --

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four months, five months. I don't remember. I didn't really -- I can't really recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that when you arrived at Prelovo, Mitar Vasiljevic was already working there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got there, and I found them there already. They were cleaning, washing the windows, cleaning the place where the stoves would be placed and they positioned them where they were supposed to be. And we had to work very quickly because the army was already on the lines and we had to prepare food for the people to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many days prior to your arrival was Mitar Vasiljevic working in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, maybe three or four days before, maybe even earlier. I didn't ask him when he came and when he started to set up the kitchen in a classroom. We cleaned it, we set things up, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the crew that worked there, let me ask you, yourself, were you considered a member of the Territorial Defence or simply a civilian that was assisting in the preparation of meals?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you were working in Prelovo, were you considered a member of the TO or were you simply considered a civilian, ordinary person, helping out by cooking?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How shall I explain? I worked in Belgrade, and then I came to the sixth anniversary of my mother's death which we were marking, and they were asking for cooks, people to work in the kitchen, and then I was mobilised in the kitchen because I was still on the record as being a member of the Visegrad military recruits rather than the Belgrade list. So I was asked to stay because I was still in their military records. I couldn't go back to my work. I had to stay. I don't know how, in which way they kept their records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you receive an official mobilisation order from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some soldiers came by and they said, "Vojinovic, they are telling you to report to Belgrade to the kitchen and to be there to be in charge of the shift for cooking. They don't have a chef. They can't find anybody." I, as an experienced cook, had a lot of experience because I worked in Belgrade in the catering industry, in the restaurant business, and that's how I ended up staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, at approximately what time each day did you finish preparing the meal at midday?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 11.00, we would finish lunch. That was supposed to go to the lines. By the time it reached the lines, it would be about 1.00 or even later, depending on the vehicles. The roads were bad and so on. You couldn't really drive quickly because it's a macadam road. There's a lot of gravel and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about some vans that were used. Did you ever see a red van that was missing its muffler and made quite a bit of noise? Did you ever a see van like that when you were at Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that we used, is it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the van that you used, was it a red van that didn't have a muffler?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was red, but -- but truth to tell, I forget. I don't really remember. I didn't really try to memorise it, and it was a long time ago. So I mean, I want to say here how it was, but I cannot say that I know something when I don't. I'm telling you the truth, and I'll tell you all that I know and that will be the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All we ask of you today is just your best memory, and I would ask you, would your best memory today be that one of vans was a small, red van?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was quite small, smaller than a proper van that belonged to the forestry department, I mean the one which took the forestry commuting workers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your memory of this van is that it was red; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any memory of it today as being loud when it was used, as if it did not have a muffler on it? Did you have any memory of that?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was down on the road. There was a school down there, but it was very muddy, so it never came near, and I can't really remember. So I can't really tell you what colour it was. I can't -- I can't be sure. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that the roads that this van would travel on were in very poor condition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And the road is still in a very poor shape because it's macadam. Nobody takes care of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be the type of road that when driving on it would be possible, especially if there was weight in the vehicle, for the bottom of the vehicle to scrape along the ground or the road? Was the road in that poor condition?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the vehicle. If it was a foreign vehicle, perhaps if it is very low, then it is possible that it comes -- that it hits all those rocks and stones there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a question about the armband that Mitar Vasiljevic wore. Do you remember whether there was any insignia on that armband?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my word, I don't remember. We were all very upset, and with all that haste -- and I'm telling you the truth. It was all hurry, hurry, hurry. So I didn't really want to know. Why did I want to look at them, what they had? My concern was -- my only worry was to prepare this food, to think what to cook, how to do it. Nothing was -- had been put in order, so it all had to come out of my head; that is, I had to think up meals and all that, and I didn't really pay much attention. It never occurred to me. Only I know that he had it, and we who came there and who helped there, he gave it to us, and he also entered the kitchen. So perhaps to avoid somebody telling you, "How can you enter the kitchen without these markings?" So perhaps he put it on himself, or perhaps the Territorial Defence issued him with that to show how things should be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the time that the kitchen was moved from Prelovo to the village of Blace. The first question I'd like you to ask -- or I'd like to ask is: Can you tell us where the village of Blace is in relation to the village of Rujiste? How close are those two villages?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Blace? I come from Blace. The kitchen was at Blace, outside, and it had a tin roof. Then we were complaining because we were attacked by flies, and there were no disinfectants or anything. We were afraid, too, that we might poison the troops. Then we were given a building. Well, it was a derelict one, because after all, it was a war and all that. But then we moved over and put it in order and got the water supply so that we could wash the spoons to avoid any infection of the troops. And I was the one who organised it mostly, to have always hot water, because we could not really get all the wood and cook it. And then one had to wash the cloth, all the rags and all the napkins and all the cloths, but that -- we put it all in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vojinovic, can you give us some idea of how far apart are the villages of Rujiste from your village of Blace? How far apart are they?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh. Well, Rujiste is further from Klasnik. Klasnik is much closer to Blace, where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximate in kilometres how far Rujiste would be from Blace?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say about 5 kilometres, because it's all uphill. You leave Blace and then you go uphill and downhill, and there is forest and streams. It's not easy to get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us and tell us, when was the kitchen moved to Blace?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything about any month. I don't know. I don't remember. I don't remember. But it was quite hot, and if you'll pardon my expression, there were hosts of flies. So there was nowhere to put meat because they were there, and all our cooking utensils. And I had to cover it all with some tin plate to avoid the infection of the troops. And we didn't know how to overcome that, and that is how they eventually sent us up there, and that is where we started to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Are you familiar with the feast, the Orthodox feast of the Holy Trinity?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us whether the kitchen was moved to Blace before or after the feast of the Holy Trinity?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Upon my soul, the dates and the memory, I can't tell you anything about this to anyone because I'm slightly upset, and my heart is not quite all right. And so -- but I'm telling you all the truth, what I know. That is how that was. But something else, anything else, I'm not going to say except what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: From your testimony, it seems that aside from your contact with Mr. Vasiljevic while he was working at Prelovo, at the times that he was not at Prelovo, you had no contact with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I didn't see him. It could have been perhaps a month or so later that in the kitchen, passing by, I heard, you know, "Mitar Vasiljevic broke his leg and he's gone to Uzice to the hospital." But I don't know where that was. I never saw him again. I knew nothing about this. My duties were in the kitchen. And about all the rest of it, I know nothing. All I was thinking about was to see that the troops did not get infected, and we were very strict about that. And as far as that is concerned, I fared well. We had no problem with disease, with anything dirty and so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's a fact, is it not, that you really aren't able to tell us anything at all about what Mitar Vasiljevic may have done after he left Prelovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite get what you meant. I missed a word in your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's apparent anyway, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm putting it to the witness, Your Honour, by ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the time that you had contact with Mr. Vasiljevic in Prelovo, you're not able to tell us anything about what Mr. Vasiljevic was doing after he left Prelovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing. Nothing. I know nothing further. He left, didn't come to see us. I only worked in the kitchen. I know nothing about anything else; who, where, what. I did that all like that from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there ever come a time when you were at Lalce that you became aware of Mr. Lindo breaking his leg?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lindo broke his leg before the war, as far as I can remember, in the company that he worked at. Something like that. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did ever there come a time when you heard about a house burning in the Mahala section of Visegrad on Pionirska Street in which a large number of people from Koritnik died? Did there ever come a time when you heard about that incident?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I hear about it from you. I didn't know that. The first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanaskovic has asked you a number of questions regarding a person by the name of (redacted) and the question that I have for you is when you made a statement to Mr. Tanaskovic in August of 2000, you did not mention (redacted) in that statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I forgot to mention him because, what shall I say, I know we were in the van, but it slipped my mind. It just slipped my mind. But he was -- sure, when Mitar left Prelovo, then they gave us that one to help us out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, when is the first time that you and Mr. Tanaskovic talked about this person (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever talking with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you and Mr. Tanaskovic -- well, how many times have you spoken to Mr. Tanaskovic in preparation for your testimony yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never talk with him until that time when I made my statement in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, after you remembered about (redacted), did you contact Mr. Tanaskovic and tell him that you had remembered that there was another person working at Prelovo by the name of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. A soldier? Soldier (redacted) or that (redacted), the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The (redacted) that you've told us about today. I'm trying to find out when is the first time you spoke with Defence about remembering this person by the name of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever talking about him until today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So until Mr. Tanaskovic asked you yesterday about (redacted), you had never before been asked about Mr. (redacted); is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, correct. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that by a court order, you were given a guarantee that you would not be arrested during the time that you are here in The Hague giving your testimony? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that word from anyone. No, I didn't. I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask anyone if you could have such a guarantee before you would come and testify in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the word that you used? I don't understand that word. What did you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever say to anyone that, "I will only go and testify if I'm promised that I won't be arrested while I'm there." Did you ever make that request to anybody?

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, nobody told us anything about that. We only got that report to come here on such and such date. But as for that, nobody told us anything. I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vojinovic. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for coming to give evidence and for the evidence that you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, whilst we're waiting for the next witness, I have before me here page 2.434 of yesterday's transcript when Mr. Lindo was asked to read from his statement, the original B/C/S statement. At the time, I had the impression that he was not exactly reading as telling us what he had intended to say. The particular sentence in issue which everybody was interested in he read out as follows, according to the English translation: "He was a sort of health inspector because he had an armband with a sign. It is the ribbon of the Red Cross." Now, that, of course, was different to the English translation, the official English translation which was provided to the Prosecution of his B/C/S statement. Bearing in mind that there are many disputes in cases here about translations, I asked to have that particular statement from the B/C/S checked by the translation people, and they have come back with a revised partial translation. I've got copies of it, but I'll read it for you, "Vasiljevic made sure the kitchen was clean, took care of the food, et cetera, and was like some kind of sanitation inspector since he wore an armband with a medical or red cross marking." I will provide you with that because I think that it is a matter of some importance in relation to that witness's evidence about what he saw the accused wearing and I'll leave it for you, the parties to do what they wish in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask what has been the practice in the past when there have been various different translations, does the Court decide on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we have to decide in the end and they have to be before us officially as exhibits. This is a revised partial translation by the official translators. It is, if I may say so, a terrible problem not only with the B/C/S languages but also sometimes with the French and the English, but probably there is a slightly loose usage of words which can be interpreted in different ways. But I think that it makes it fairly clear that the witness was not reading precisely from his statement at the time, because the translation which we received is different to everything. Not perhaps in substance too much, but nevertheless, it is different. It was because I had hoped that he would read it and we would get these interpreters' translation of it that I was concerned that he clearly was not reading it from the way in which he was interpolating his own recollection and to some extent a self-justification. Now, that's one matter I want to raise at this stage. The other matter relates to this issue of doctors. At the end of your cross-examination, Mr. Groome, you put to the accused this, and I'm reading from 2240 of the transcript:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't it true that you did not break your leg falling from a horse but that you broke your leg on the steep and slippery bank of the creek by the house that was on fire? Mr. Vasiljevic then answered:

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I've understood you. You say I broke the leg by the house that was set on fire. And the question was repeated:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, isn't it a fact, isn't the truth that you broke your leg slipping during the commission of the crime against those people when you went around the back of the house and you fell on the steep and slippery bank of the creek? To which Mr. Vasiljevic replied:

utterances.speaker: VASILIJE VOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a pure fabrication, sir. Now, it seems to me, Mr. Groome, that the case of the Prosecution has altered somewhat. It's not a question of whether that he was ever in hospital in Uzice and for some weeks having his broken leg treated, but the issue is when he broke his leg, which of course also involves where. And the Prosecution -- I'm sorry, the Defence have something like eight witnesses to come along to say he was at the hospital in Uzice. Now, I think we're going to have to sort out what is the real issue in this case about this, because if we have to listen to eight witnesses coming along simply to say he was in hospital at Uzice when the Prosecution's case is not that he wasn't or that it wasn't a reasonable possibility that he was but simply that if he did break his leg, it was at a different time of day and at a different place, but it nevertheless happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not exactly clear on what you're asking me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm asking you what your case is. Because if your case is simply that if he did break his leg it was at a different time of day, so that there is still -- you can still establish that he was at the house, then we do not need eight people from the Uzice hospital to say he spent some weeks in that hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to it. The Prosecution has to establish, as part of its case, at least on one version of its case, that he was at the Pionirska Street fire. That's the way you put that highest part of your case. You put an alternative that if we weren't satisfied beyond reasonable doubt about that, he nevertheless participated in the whole business at some earlier stage of the day. But let's take your highest case, that he was at the house that was burnt and at the time it was burning in Pionirska Street. Now, in answer to that case, the accused raises an alibi. He has no burden of proof in relation to that alibi. He simply has to be able to point to the evidence. And he points to evidence that he was admitted into hospital, first of all in the local hospital, and then he was transferred to the Uzice hospital. And he says he broke his leg, and there's going to be some evidence to support what he said, apparently, that he broke it during the course of the afternoon and, therefore, could not have been at the house at the time it was burning. Now, if there is a reasonable possibility that he was injured earlier in the afternoon, then clearly we cannot be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that he was at the house at the time it was burning. You bear the onus of proving that notwithstanding the evidence he produces, that he was at the house at the time it was burning. Now, the Defence have nominated, I think it is eight witnesses, which are there to meet Dr. De Grave's evidence that the man whose leg was X-rayed at the Uzice hospital is not the accused. It seems, from what was said yesterday, that there is some doubt about Dr. De Grave's evidence. You referred to the fact that you'd given a report to Mr. Domazet for him to use for whatever purpose he wishes. He has described it as having a considerably different result to Dr. De Grave's evidence. Now, I think that we are entitled to know what is the Prosecution case in the light of your cross-examination of the accused, where you put to him that he broke his leg not riding a horse during the afternoon but slipping down the greasy slope between the two houses at the time the house was burning. What is the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court has heard not only Dr. De Grave say that the X-rays did not match but also that the break was consistent -- the break that he saw on Mr. Vasiljevic was consistent with somebody slipping and falling on such a steep embankment. The Court has also heard from three witnesses that mister -- one witness placing Mr. Vasiljevic directly behind the house, at the time of the fire, on that steep embankment. Also, from another -- at least one other witness that he was by the Omeragic house as the people were transferred there and from several other witnesses who put him there at the time that the fire began. The Court would be entitled to assess their credibility and infer, I believe, that Mr. Vasiljevic was in fact there and that the explanation for his broken leg was that something happened during the course of the crime in which he broke his leg and then was subsequently treated at Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But is this because you are not going to attempt to establish that there was no reasonable possibility that he broke his leg and was in the Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to attempt to establish that he was not in Uzice hospital at the time that the fire -- that the actual fire was set and those people were burnt to death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it's an issue of time, not that he was there. You see, if we accept Dr. De Grave's evidence, then clearly it was not Mr. Vasiljevic who was in the hospital at all, and it's in answer to that case that these eight witnesses are going to be brought along to say that he was there. But your case seems to have changed so that the issue is not whether he was there at all but what time did he get there. And if that is so, it would be a complete waste of time for the Defence to bring eight witnesses to say that he was there for some weeks having his leg treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess I'm thinking what is the alternative. What is the Court seeking from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm asking you what your case is. Now, I don't want to say that again. That's the third time I've put it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think I've articulated what the Prosecution case is regarding Defence witnesses. The Prosecution certainly isn't prepared to stipulate or agree that Mr. Vasiljevic was in the hospital at 9.30 that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not asking you to. I'm asking you whether it is necessary, in order to meet your case, for them to bring eight witnesses who will simply say he spent four weeks or some particular period of time at the Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't see how I can answer that question, Your Honour. I know that the doctors that are coming are not the doctors who filled out the medical records. I know certain things --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Groome, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That point is -- you're being asked to slow down. No doubt we are not pausing between our responses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask this? Could I just ask for a few minutes to think about this, and maybe at the end of the session or at the beginning of the next session, maybe we can discuss it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Mr. Groome. I don't want to put you on a spot if you want to think about it. But it seems to me, at least, that it will be a complete waste of time for the Defence to bring along eight witnesses to say that he spent this time at the hospital if you are putting a case that he got there much later than he said he was and he could still have been at the house at the time it was burning. In those circumstances, the only doctors who would need to be called would be those -- or nurses who could say they saw him there at a particular time, and perhaps his uncle who is going to be called, as I recall, to explain that they stopped off along the way for a drink on the way to Uzice, and probably the ambulance driver who took him to the local hospital. But we are not here just to allow people to play games. We are entitled to insist upon the real issue being litigated. And if the real issue does not include a Prosecution case that it could not have been Mr. Vasiljevic at the hospital at all, as it started out to be, then there would obviously be a great savings of time if the statements by these doctors, et cetera, were tendered and they didn't have to be brought here. Now, that's what I'm trying to do, is to bring the parties down to a real issue in the case. Unfortunately, for too long this Tribunal has allowed the parties to have their heads and just fight anything, but the Rules have been altered, and we are entitled to insist upon the real issue being litigated. Now, it's up to the Prosecution, then, to tell us now what they see to be the real issue about the entry by Mr. Vasiljevic into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Of course, a very loud inference can be drawn from the statement that you have sent your new expert's report on the X-ray to Mr. Domazet for him to do what he wishes with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, rather than the Court draw any inference from my statement, I would be happy to provide the report to the Court. I didn't because it seems to me that until it was in evidence, it would have been inappropriate to put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you're required to file them 21 days in advance. We obviously see them before the witnesses are called.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll have a copy to that after the next session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can tell you exactly what is in the report now if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. What is in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The report is an inconsistent finding. The report says that the small bone in the leg was not broken on the X-ray but that the break in the large bone is compatible with the healed fracture of Mr. Vasiljevic's bone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's a very different case then, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour. I still want to speak to the expert and study -- and speak with him. The report is very brief and very conclusionary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If that's so, we will certainly give you every opportunity to consider what your case is, but you can see if Dr. De Grave, whose evidence was not produced with ease, to say the least of it, if he is not going to be relied upon because there's a reasonable doubt as to the accuracy of his report or his evidence, then the case is very different, isn't it, and there will be no need for the Defence to prove simply that he was in hospital and we will save eight witnesses, which is about a week's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Have we got the other witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, will you please make the solemn declaration in the document that the court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court your particulars, your first and last name, where you are from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Simic and I was born in Visegrad in a village close to Visegrad called Haluga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was born on November 26, 1950.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your profession, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I am a school teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a school teacher in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been living in Visegrad, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was born in Visegrad, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were born in a village near Visegrad and that you live in Visegrad and I thought, perhaps, that you moved to Visegrad later.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lived in another village in the village of Prelovo because of my work. That's where I -- I worked in a school in that area, and then I moved to Visegrad in 1992 in December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you know Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that person in the courtroom right now? Did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't see him at the moment. Yes. Yes. Yes. I can see him. He's there behind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think we can all agree that he has now identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Simic, how long have you known Mitar Vasiljevic, since whence do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I came to work in that area in 1969 so that means that I know him from 1971 approximately. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Simic, something about 1992, about the period which you probably remember? Was the Uzice Corps in Visegrad at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in Visegrad sometime until perhaps the 19th or the 20th of May, and then it left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in that period, Mr. Simic, before the Uzice Corps arrived in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was a turbulent time. The situation was tense. People on both sides were arming themselves. I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that the Uzice Corps was in Visegrad, was the situation better or worse?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: With the arrival of the Corps, the situation calmed down. I even went to my own house. I think I continued to work in the school in that area. I don't know for how long, maybe for 10 or 15 days, but I think that schools started to work again and the situation became a little calmer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which school did you work in, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I worked in the elementary school Zelimir Djuric Zeljo in Prelovo. Actually, it was an outpost of the school in Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened, particularly with you, after the Uzice Corps left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: With the departure of the Uzice Corps, I received a call to report to the school and I was allocated to a unit there because I was in communications in the army. I received the same duties then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, when you say, "I was told to report to the school," which school do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: To the building of the elementary school at Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building where the school was, was it used as a school at that time or was it used for some other purpose?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember that. It was a long time ago. I know that we worked for a while, but I don't know up until when. I'm not able to say that right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's possible that I didn't formulate my question properly. Since you said that you were told to report to a school, you're a teacher, did you report to the school in order to teach or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Oh, I understand now. I didn't come to work. I came to report there just like the other people did who were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a mobilisation, it was a call-up in accordance with which you reported to the school in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We all reported there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the people who were with you at the school at that time, that first day that you reported there for your call-up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It would be a long list. There were many of us, perhaps 150. I don't remember exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you specifically this: The kitchen that served the mobilised people, was it set up there in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The kitchen was there and there was also a small first aid unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was there in those first days? Who was there in the kitchen and around the kitchen, in the kitchen itself, supplying the kitchen, doing cleaning duties and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Vojinovic Vaso was there, Dragisa Lindo, Mitar Vasiljevic, Obren Vojnovic, and another person, Mitrasin, I can't remember his last name right now, Glisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what you know or saw that a particular person's duties were at that time? Let's start with Vaso Vojinovic who you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Vaso Vojinovic was a cook there. He was preparing food for the soldiers. I think that he was probably called up because he was most probably a cook in the army so that's why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dragisa Lindo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Dragisa Lindo was a helper. He would distribute food, peel potatoes, sort the beans. He was a helper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic was also a cook, but I'm not exactly sure whether he cooked or whether he helped, but I know that he used to go and get the food supplies in a van that we had. He would bring the supplies and then he would also go out into the field to distribute the food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Obren Vojinovic whom you mentioned, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Obren Vojinovic drove the van, and he used to drive that same van in the forestry department before the war, and that's why he was assigned to that duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that he was a professional driver in the forestry department before the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the forestry department, what is that? Is that a company or some other institution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It's a company that cultivates and preserves and also deals with forest exploitation. They deal with forestation, also protection from fires and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Obren Vojinovic was a driver at the forestry department before the war, and he drove the van then that he used to drive in Prelovo at that time. Does that mean that the vehicle was also requisitioned for those purposes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned a little while ago as one of Mitar's duties to go with the van to get food supplies, did you mean that he used that van or another van? Are you saying that Mitar Vasiljevic drove that van?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no. We would go to get supplies from the town using that van, and we used that van as well in order to distribute food. And the only person who drove the van was Obren Vojinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they would go with the van to get the food supplies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: They used to go to town, to Visegrad. I think there was a kind of central warehouse for all that, all of that area. That's what I think, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were called up and told to report to this school in Prelovo. Do you know if this was also the case for all the other people that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: They were all called up and told to report there, all of them. Probably all of them were born in that area, and that is probably the reason why they were told to report precisely where they were told to report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally wear a uniform at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a uniform of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It's a uniform of the SMB colour; a shirt, trousers, and there was also a cap, a hat. Some took that hat, and some did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get that uniform when you got to Prelovo or did you have it at your house as a member of the reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I had the uniform from earlier on. I had signed for it because I was a member of the reserves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it usual at that time for JNA reservists to keep that uniform at home?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: A certain number of people did keep it at home, maybe everybody who was in the reserves, but not everybody who had reported there had a uniform. Many of them arrived wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mitar Vasiljevic was wearing a uniform the first time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing the same uniform. I don't think he was wearing any kind of cap or hat, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "The same kind of uniform," do you mean the uniform that you had, the uniform of the former JNA, the SMB, the olive-grey colour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I mean. The olive-grey coloured uniform of the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him for the first time then, did you notice if he had any weapons with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I noticed him on the first day or the second day, but he did have a weapon. I think it was an automatic rifle. I don't know whether it was a German or a Russian weapon, but I know that we called it a Schmeisser.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw him with that weapon the first time that you saw him, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but you don't know whether that was the first day or the second day, if I've understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later, while you were both at Prelovo, did you see what kind of a weapon Mitar had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he carried that Schmeisser, because that weapon was most appropriate because he was going in and out of the kitchen and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were discussing what you know about his duties, except when you mentioned that he would go to get supplies to town, you also said that he would go out to the lines to distribute food.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, did you personally see how food was taken to the lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I remember. For lunch, we would take a cooked meal. Sometimes there would be a double portion so that there would be cooked food for dinner as well. Sometimes we would take dry food instead -- along with the cooked food to be used for dinner. Sometimes we would take cooked -- a cooked meal for dinner and for lunch. For breakfast, we also took some food and also tea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, when you say, "We took the food," does that mean that you also did that always or occasionally went to the line, you personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need for me to go to the lines with them. Three of them were enough to distribute the food, and also the driver would help them. Sometimes I did go, though, but for -- because of other work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you remember whether the soldiers who were there, including all of you, carried any kind of insignia, any kind of characteristic insignia which they would be distinguished by?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, but for two days, not longer than that. Less than two days we carried insignia tied to the epaulettes on our shoulders. They were thin ribbons in different colours. They were issued to us, and they were used in case somebody who we didn't know would enter into our unit, even though this was not necessary because we all knew each other. And we were issued with these ribbons. And then we did receive a kind of code, according to which we would wear a certain ribbon on a certain day. To tell you the truth, I didn't wear this ribbon very often. Everybody knew me, so I moved about freely and very often. I was without such a ribbon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you very well, it was a thin ribbon that you wore on the epaulettes, on your shoulder of your uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "different colours," does that mean on certain days or for a certain period you were supposed to wear only one colour or was it permitted to wear a different colour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. As far as I would remember, we would change them every day. We would get a message in the evening, for example, that tomorrow it would be yellow. The next day it would be red. To tell you the truth, I never changed my ribbon. I think the cook, Vaso, also never changed his ribbon, because we never went out. The people who were out on the field -- in the field and who moved around a lot, they would change the ribbons frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, the people who were out in the field needed to take care of this, to pay attention to this so that they would be recognised by soldiers on the same side.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Those people who were out in the field and who would go back and forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you explained, these were very small, narrow ribbons which were worn on the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were perhaps 1 centimetre wide and perhaps 8 or 10 centimetres long. Ten, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps we can move to the other sized ribbon after the adjournment. We will return at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, before the break, you explained to us how all those who were at Prelovo had those shoulder ribbons and you gave a detailed explanation about that. My next question is if any other of people around you had perhaps some ribbons or armbands of a different colour than you described and if yes, then who did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The male nurse and Mitar had those -- wore armbands, whether on the left arm or the right arm, I'm not quite sure, I think it was the right arm, and they were about 8 centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw the nurse or nurses wearing an armband of some kind and Mitar Vasiljevic. Were these identical armbands in both cases, and could you please describe those armbands if you remember them, of course?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The size was the same, but the colour wasn't. The nurses or rather there was just one male nurse, and he had a white armband with a red cross and to his -- on the door to his room, there was also a red cross so that people would know where the infirmary was whereas Mitar had a red armband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that armband which Mitar had on his arm, and you tell us it was red, were there any other emblems on that armband?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not quite sure but I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from -- you told us that now and then, Mitar and the driver went to the town to get foodstuffs. Would you know if Mitar Vasiljevic left Prelovo privately, that is, not officially or rather did Mitar Vasiljevic go home now and then? Would you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: All of us, and that includes Mitar, would go home now and then to have a bath, for a change of clothes, and then we would be back. At times it would be for a night. At times for a few hours only, and come back, and that goes for Mitar too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how did he go home on those occasions when he went home?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess like everybody else. Sometimes using these delivery vans, at times in a car would come up. Those who lived nearby would just walk. It depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mitar Vasiljevic could drive, and did he ever own a car at any time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I never saw him drive a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say this about him or anybody else, that it depended how they would go home, that is either on foot or getting a lift from anybody, is that it; did I understand you well? Does that go for Mitar too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That was Mitar's case too. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Prelovo from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: About 9 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Mitar Vasiljevic's house is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I do, in the village of Blace, that was where he was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where he lives now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know that too, where his family is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that house on the Prelovo-Visegrad road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It is nearer to Visegrad, perhaps about 2 kilometres or maybe a kilometre out of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that, you mean, I presume, the centre of Visegrad when you give us these distances?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That's how I -- that is how I figured it out, yes, from the centre of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about this van that belonged to the forestry enterprise that was driven by Obren Vojinovic, do you remember what kind of a van was it and, in particular, do you remember its colour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was a van used to transport the forestry company workers to work and from it. Obren drove that vehicle before the war for quite some time, I think. What colour it was, well, orange or red, I'm not quite sure. I think it was a Maribor make, but I know it was the forestry company because Obren used to joke. "When all this is over, and it will be over, then that van will again be my livelihood."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "to transport workers," do you mean that there were more seats in it than usually there are in a van or do you remember what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I think it could take 8 or 9, perhaps 2 or 3 seats more, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long was Mitar Vasiljevic with you at Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: About 10 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why not longer than that or, rather, do you know where he went after those 10 or so days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't. I know that he left and he did not turn up again, whether he was assigned to some other place or what, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later on overhear what had happened to him and where he was, where he'd been?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really care to know about that. I mean, you know, there were lots of people there. All I know is that he ended up in the hospital with a broken leg. And I wouldn't have -- that wouldn't have registered either had I not known through conversation that he had fallen off a horse. And you know, there were many people injured at that time, so who would remember it all. But people had said that he'd fallen off a horse, and that sounded funny, so that's why I registered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, after those ten or so days at Prelovo when he left, you did not see him again in the months that followed, to make it quite precise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I did not see him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, as soon as Mitar Vasiljevic was arrested, you saw it in the media. So how did you react to that since you knew him before and after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't find that out from the media. But that is a kind of a story which circulates very quickly, so I heard it from other people, and I was quite surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that you were surprised? That is, why were you taken aback by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, because I know Mitar. He was quite a merry man and -- because of his profession. And anyway, he always socialised with people, and I found it difficult to believe that he had done anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that from what you knew about him, you thought it wasn't likely that he could have done such a thing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Groome. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic. My name is Dermot Groome. I'm representing the Prosecution here, and I'll ask you a few questions regarding your testimony. How long did you yourself work in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In Prelovo and schools around Prelovo since 1969.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you first begin to work or how long did you work in Prelovo with respect to this cooking duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Oh, that's what you mean. I didn't prepare any food. I was a signals man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've testified that at one point, Mitar Vasiljevic stopped coming to work at Prelovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you ever informed why a member of the crew was no longer going to be assigned or be working in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know it, and I didn't really want to know. It was none of my business. There were 100, 150, sometimes 200 people. Perhaps he was doing some job for the army. So ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were on the crew, the cooking crew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Five. Well, four at times, and at times five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we've heard from other witnesses on that crew that Mitar Vasiljevic had a somewhat -- his capacity was somewhat of a supervisor or an inspector. Would you agree with that characterisation of his job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, since he wore this armband, I suppose, yes, he was -- he was a boss there. Because he didn't really cook. He was mostly engaged in procuring food, and Vaso was the one who was the chief cook. But then on the other hand, when the cooking was over, when the food would be prepared, Vaso would be a free man again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when this person who had these responsibilities stopped showing up for work, there was never an explanation as to why. Is that what you're testifying to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose somebody had been notified about his absence and the reasons for it, but not me. And had I wanted to know, I could have asked, I guess, but there were so many people coming and going that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before he left, did Mr. Vasiljevic ever say to you that he had concerns or fears about going to the front line and delivering food? Did he ever say anything like that to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not that I remember. But you know, we were all quite apprehensive, because those 10, maybe 20 kilometres away from the kitchen to reach the front lines. I don't remember him complaining ever to me, but I was also quite fearful when I had to cover that area. You know, that ground is not very nice. There are very many curves. There are boulders and wooded areas, so that none of us were particularly happy about it because it was a dangerous journey indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, sir, is as you sit here today, can you recollect any time that Mr. Vasiljevic said to you, "I have" -- that he was afraid of going to the front line to distribute the food?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I cannot recollect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after Mitar Vasiljevic left Prelovo, would it be fair to say that you did not see him again for quite some time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't. I didn't often go to the town because my family was in Prelovo. So after 15 or maybe 20 days, I even moved further on. So I'd come to Prelovo. I'd get home, have a bath, change, and leave. I never went into town. There was no need for me to go there. Perhaps once in 20 days or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your work as a teacher, did you have occasion to teach a person by the name of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Milan Lukic is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I used to see him around town after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know that his name was Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
