utterances.text: Yes. I know there was a Muslim there in the same hospital, but I just don't know his name. He was in a bed next to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know anything about their relations, were there any problems? Were they in trouble between the two of them? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to what I asked you a moment ago. Do you remember something specific, any detail about those ramblings of your husband when you said that you had concluded that he was ranting that something was wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just could realise what he was saying was nonsense. "We'll live there. We'll live there." I could immediately see that something was wrong. He didn't even ask about children, and he doted on them. He always asked about them. He always inquired after them, and on that occasion, he never said a word, and that is when I suggested that he should perhaps go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did his behaviour on that occasion remind you of the way that he behaved after those drinking bouts and binges? Did it look anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, in a way, except that it was more of that. But yes, there were similar situations before, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he came out of the hospital at your request.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the doctors were not for discharging him from the hospital and that you requested that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is true. The doctors opposed it. But I signed that I would -- that I was taking him home, because he was really ranting. He didn't know. He wasn't aware of anything that was happening around him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then sign that you were assuming the risk, that you were doing it under your own responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is right. I wanted to take him home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else with you when you came to get him from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His uncle came, Dobrivoje Sikric. And we took him out of the hospital at my initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you take him then?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I took him back home. But I had to take care that he took his medicines regularly and what medicines he took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he take them all?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He took all his medicines under my supervision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did his health, I mean mental health, improve after he returned home?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes. No doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he still in a plaster cast? You said a leg-long plaster cast. That is what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long did he have this cast?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: For a very long time. We went for check-ups every 15 to 20 days, and the doctors said when it had to be shorter. So for a while it was down to the knee. Then after that, they cut it further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take him for controls both to the orthopaedic surgeon and to doctors who were taking care of his mental state?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, both the orthopaedic surgeon and those others, because we had exactly the schedule when he had to report for controls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did these examinations take place?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: In Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before going to Uzice, did he have to go for a control in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He would first go to a doctor in Visegrad, and they'd give the piece of paper and then he'd go to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in Visegrad, you would be given a document, a referral document to go to a doctor in Uzice. Is that what you say -- what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember and did you see what kind of a fracture did your husband suffer?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that he broke his leg, but how, I don't know. Whether both bones or one, I don't know. We had the X-rays, but we were moving house, we lost it. Had I known this would happen, I would of course have looked after it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was about to ask you that. Did you have these X-rays at home?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we must have had them. Of course we did have them. But we moved house and, I suppose, misplaced them somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long, as far as you can remember, how long was he treated for this fracture?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: A long time. A very long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "long," does it mean several months?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. It took several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after he recovered, what did he do then?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot remember. I know he broke his leg again in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to ask you that. Will you explain to me what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He broke his leg again in 1993, on the 6th of May, the same leg. We were at the Slava at his father's, and he broke the same leg, except three centimetres below the first fracture or above the first fracture. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the 6th of May and the Slava, what Slava is that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is St. George's Day, the 6th of May, at the father's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did Mitar Vasiljevic's father live?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Dzurevici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the second fracture happened in Dzurevici?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he taken for treatment?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: To Uzice once again, except that they did not apply weights, because he knew that he wasn't supposed to move and he didn't, and they did not have to put the two fragments of bone together. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean that on that second occasion he was hospitalised for a much shorter time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He wasn't there for 21 days. He did not have to carry this weight. There was no need to put his leg in extension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, did he need crutches?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was -- he was again in the plaster cast, except that it wasn't that -- that big as the first time. And he again had to go for check-ups. And after all that, he went to a spa in 1993. The first time he didn't go to a spa because the spa was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the spa," do you mean rehabilitation?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's it. After the fracture in 1993, he went for rehabilitation, that is, when the leg was all right. It was then that he went to a spa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did he undergo any noteworthy operations again?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1994, he had his spine operated in Belgrade. I think it was the 16th of June, 1994, in Zemun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, was he treated; that is, did he undergo rehabilitation?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that treatment lasted a little longer, in a spa, and then there were further controls for about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if after that, after he had recovered from that surgery, if after that he was wounded, he suffered that mishap? Could you explain what it was about?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he received a wound in his leg, quite by accident. I was visiting his parents in his village, and they called me to let me know that he was at the hospital in Sokolac. And then I think he had injured the middle toe on his left foot, but I'm not sure about which one exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how it happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think he went -- no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or rather was it somebody else who injured him or did he injure himself?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He did it himself. He had picked up a rifle to move it and that rifle fired and hit him in his toe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasiljevic, I am going to finish now by moving on to another subject. In the beginning of your testimony today, you said that you had graduated from the secondary commercial school and started to work. Since many witnesses have already said that they saw you at your place of work, I would like you, if you can, please tell us or mention for us all the places that you worked and the periods when you worked there.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I started to work as full-time staffer in 1985. I worked in Prelovo, Sase, in all parts of the town. I worked in Crnca, Dusce, I worked at the department store and also at all of the UPI stores.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us that in some kind of order, and I'm interested particularly in the period up until 1992? Because what you have just said, this period that you are talking about is before 1992. So could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked at Prelovo, Sase, Crnca, Dusce, and in all of the UPI stores in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned Sase, did you know a man by the name of (redacted) (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him well. I worked not far from his house, perhaps 100 or 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything that you know about him in a little more detail from that period?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He liked to drink and he would always stick around in the shop. He would drink and sing, make merry. He would always greet me, say hello to me. I knew his whole family. Sometimes he would drop by with Mitar for a drink because he worked at Terpentin. He would always celebrate Mitar's day and he said, "If I was a Serb, I would be called Mitar." He always also used to treat us when we were at the store.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he came to the store, tell us, was it a custom for people to drink in the store?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right. And he would always treat everybody. He also used to stop by with Mitar and they would have a drink or stop by with company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mean in the store as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at Sase where I worked. He would drop by after work if we would -- the store would still be open because we merchants would keep our shops open a little longer so then he would stay until closing time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that he said that he was born on the 8th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The 8th of November is Serbian Slava, Mitar's day, so Mitar was named after that. Well, he never worked on that day and he said, "If I were a Serb, I would be called Mitar." And he never worked on that day, he would just go around and celebrate. He would treat people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me something about Mitar's family? Did he have any brothers and sisters and if he did, who, where did they live, were they older or younger than him?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Mitar was the eldest child of his parents, and he had two younger sisters and the youngest brother, and he also had a half-sister. His brother lived in Belgrade and he lives there to this day. His sisters, one of them is in Belgrade, one of them is in Prelovo, and the other one is in Vardiste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that he had a half-sister; is that a half-sister from his father or from his mother's side?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is a half-sister on his father's side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that he lost his mother or that his father divorced his mother?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Mitar lost his mother when he was a young boy. His mother disappeared when Mitar was perhaps 8 years old. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So his father got married again and so this half-sister is from his father's second marriage, if I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is his stepmother still alive today?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now something about the families' kums, that you entered into these kum relationships between the family that you married into, the Vasiljevic family, and the Lukic family. What do you know about this kum relationship?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The families Lukic and Vasiljevic are -- have a kum relationship, and this relationship is maybe 100 or 200 years old. It was passed down from generation to generation, and in our custom, it is not something that should be broken because in our belief, if somebody happens, if you break off a kumship, then if something bad happens, it can be interpreted that it happened because of that. So the kumship is passed down from father to son, so the oldest son inherits this relationship. If there is no son, then the daughter can inherit this relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this particular case, your husband's family, the kumship was taken over by -- inherited by his father, Ljubo. According to tradition, Mitar, as the oldest son, was supposed to carry it on.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, that's how it works. The oldest male child would inherit this relationship from the father, and then it is passed down to the next generation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are running over without any regard to the translation. You must pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his brother, and you said this was his younger brother, where did he live?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: His younger brother lived and still lives in Belgrade, and he went to Belgrade as soon as he finished school. That's where he lives and he works there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now about some people from that family, the Lukic family, that the Vasiljevic family was in a kum relationship with. I would first of all like to ask you about Milan Lukic. Do you know who Milan Lukic is?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because his father is the eldest kum so of course I know about him. I know that he has four children. I don't know them all. I only know one son. Afterwards when the war started, I saw Milan once or twice. I never seen him before. I don't know where he was. I still don't know the other two children. I think they are somewhere abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question because in this way, you said something that I'm afraid I didn't understand too well and I probably think others didn't understand it too. So let's do this properly. When you said, "I know he had four children," who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Our kum, Milan Lukic's father, had several children. So of course I know Milan, but I never saw him before. So when we were talking about the old kum, how many children he said, I never saw Milan. And until the war broke out, I didn't know where he was or what he was doing. I only saw him two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you said that until the war, you never saw Milan Lukic and that he wasn't in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please slow down. When you say "up until the war," do you mean this period in 1992 which we talked about? Do you remember when you saw him for the first time and on which occasions you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I saw him once when Mitar broke his leg. He came to visit him for about five minutes. Maybe sometimes as he was passing by on his way to work. I never spent any time with him. I never sat down with him or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he came to your house before Mitar was hurt on the Holy Trinity day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he never did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a few minutes ago that Mitar said that towards the end of his stay in Prelovo, Milan Lukic brought him home. On that occasion did he come up to the house and did you see him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Mitar just told me that, and I didn't. No. Mitar told me, but I didn't see him personally. Perhaps I was at work or I was out of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later, when Mitar told you about something that happened to his colleague, and you explained that in a little bit more detail, did he mention Milan Lukic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Mitar only mentioned something. He was ranting, talking. I wasn't there, so I don't know what happened. When he came home, he was talking without making any sense, that it was something about his colleague and his colleague's son and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who brought him home on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, did you personally see or did you hear from Mitar whether after what you just said - until the time he was injured and taken to the Uzice hospital, do you know whether in that period he saw Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether perhaps at weddings or some kind of celebration if Mitar saw him, but he never came to our house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you didn't understand my question. My question relates to only the period from that day when he came home, and you said he was ranting and talking without any sense, until the time he went to the Uzice hospital. So in that period.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Stanko Pecikoza?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He made all the doors and the windows on our house, and he was also our neighbour. He was one of the best men in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what he did? What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He had his own personal store. He was a carpenter. He also cut construction material. He was also a very good host, a very good man. He took care of his household.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. They -- they worked for a while. We didn't have enough money to make the windows and the doors on our house, so he did that, and then Mitar worked for him in order to pay off his debt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that Mitar worked in his shop, and in return he received the doors and the windows to the house that you were building.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Before the war, he made our balcony doors and the windows, and he was supposed to make something else. Unfortunately, he was killed, so he didn't get to do it. But his son did that afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did his son do?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, Stanko made the windows for our balcony, our front door, and he was supposed to make another external front door. Unfortunately, in the meantime, he was killed, so then his son made those doors after, afterwards, after he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, did you hear how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how he was killed. I think somebody killed him and they found him somewhere in a car, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That evening when Mitar came and he talked about Meho and all the other things, did he mention Stanko Pecikoza at that time? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mitar met Stanko somewhere in town. I don't know where. And he said he was looking for Milan, and they went towards Vilina Vlas to look for Milan. They went to Banja together, and Mitar came back from there. I don't know who brought him back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you found this out from Mitar, from his story, from what he told you?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Stanko Pecikoza, whom you described as a wealthy and very good man and businessman, employed his Muslim neighbours and protected them?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whoever wanted to work could get a job from him and have enough money to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to go back and discuss a few more things about Milan Lukic. Do you know that your Mitar was his best man, his witness at his wedding? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Just in passing, since Mitar is the oldest child and according to our beliefs a kum should not be changed, my father-in-law was out in the village, away, he was sick, so he met Mitar, and of course he wanted to have him as a kum. He wouldn't change. I wasn't there, so I don't know when this happened. Mitar and another witness - I don't know who it was - went to attend his wedding ceremony, and it took 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that afterwards, after the wedding, or were you told before the wedding?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard it after the wedding, because according to our beliefs in our nation, an offer of kumship is never refused no matter who it is. An offer to be somebody's kum is never refused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear who else attended the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mitar ever tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that later, Mitar was the godfather at his daughter's christening? And if this happened, were you also present?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The child was christened on the 27th or the 28th in 1996 or 1997. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at the christening?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, just Mitar and the children, because I was at work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only reason why you didn't attend the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't be absent from work because there weren't enough workers at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that this was a work day?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period, did you know somebody who had the same name, first name as your husband Mitar, but his last name is Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was working in Prelovo, that's where he was born. I never saw him personally, but he appeared out of nowhere from -- during the war. However, before the war, I never saw him but during the war, he sort of appeared. I don't know where he came from. And sometimes in passing on my way to work, he wore a big fur hat, he had a beard. He didn't have one eye, and he looked pretty terrible, and that's why I noticed him. I don't remember where he was, but I -- the only thing I remember is that he just appeared from somewhere during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except for that, you seeing him, did you ever hear from anybody that he did something that wasn't allowed?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. I heard that he did commit or do a lot of things that are not supposed to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you didn't see, but can you please tell us what you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard that he took part in house burning, but I don't know. I wasn't there. I didn't see it. Ugly things, but I don't remember what were all the things that he did. --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "ugly things," can you tell us or -- I mean you said you don't remember. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: -- I heard from people that he did all kinds of things, but I can't remember all the things that he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other soldiers or paramilitaries, unofficial formations around who also did ugly things as you said? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that there were also paramilitaries, but I don't know who did what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mitar Knezevic one of those people, according to what you heard?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the same name that he shared with your husband, did he resemble your husband in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He had a beard. He had a big black hat, subara, a fur hat, he didn't have one eye. His nickname was "Chetnik."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that you mention the hat, did your husband have a hat that he would wear occasionally?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps occasionally a small hat, but perhaps he wore it occasionally, a small hat, but he didn't wear it every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, may I suggest that you ask the witness what was the fur hat that Mitar Knezevic wore, what was the shape of it. I think I can understand what a fur hat is, but I think we should have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not one in any way like the ones we have had described, that's the problem, but I think we better have it properly described somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He wore a subara, and there was a kind of marking on it. I don't know how to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court what is a subara? What kind of a hat?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a longer, bigger thing on your head. It's black, and it had a marking, insignia on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I think what we need to know is whether it has a brim. I don't think it does, but I think we better get it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That hat, subara, that you saw on Mitar Knezevic's head, does it have a brim?

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The subara can be worn straight up, but you can also fold it back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try it like this: The brim is something that you have on a hat and it can be wide or narrow; does a subara have such a brim? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know. A subara is -- everybody knows what a subara is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you know, but maybe somebody here in the courtroom doesn't know, so could you please explain what the difference is between a subara and what we call a hat.

utterances.speaker: MILOJKA VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: A subara is bigger and longer. It's a tall hat. You can wear it unfolded so that it's tall, but you can also fold is so that it has a little piece around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't know what sort of an artist your witness is but it might be an idea if she drew it. My understanding of it, and I may be very wrong, I think I'm thinking of a Russian hat, it will have some sort of a flap that you can fold down over your ears, but it does not have a brim. I think we better get it clear, but we'll come back to it in the morning. We'll adjourn now until 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: at 4.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday the 16th day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
